claims.text: A high-throughput computational screening method can be used to design intrinsically strong, ductile, low-density refractory high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method integrates density functional theory, machine-learning interatomic potentials, and thermodynamic and kinetic modeling.
The method optimizes lattice distortion and phase stability to balance intrinsic strength and ductility.
The candidate space includes multi-principal refractory alloys containing Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and W in various proportions.
The framework can screen a broad compositional space for predicted strength, ductility, and weight reduction.
Machine-learning-potential simulations can examine refractory-alloy behavior from ambient to high temperatures.
Computationally selected alloys would subsequently be synthesized and tested under controlled laboratory conditions.
Optimized atomic arrangements and phase distributions can include stable solid solutions or finely dispersed nanoscale precipitates.
The optimized phase distributions mitigate brittle-phase formation.
Atomic ordering can alter dislocation motion in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Composition can be correlated with lattice distortion and phase stability to predict mechanically favorable alloys.
Incorporating lighter refractory elements reduces overall alloy density.
The selected compositions can retain or enhance load-bearing capacity despite their lower density.
Favorable dislocation interactions produced by composition selection improve ductility.
Designed RHEAs will have yield strengths comparable to or greater than conventional MoNbTaTiW.
Designed RHEAs will have improved ductility and reduced mass relative to conventional MoNbTaTiW.
Equimolar MoNbTaTiW is a conventional refractory high-entropy-alloy benchmark.
Conventional equimolar MoNbTaTiW typically has relatively high density and limited ductility.
The method's effectiveness is limited by the accuracy of its interatomic potentials and thermodynamic databases.
Experimental synthesis may produce microstructures that differ from computational predictions.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome allows yield strength merely comparable to the benchmark, whereas the falsification rule requires a statistically significant yield-strength improvement; a result satisfying the stated prediction could therefore be classified as falsifying it.
